Hi, thank you for fitting me in. Um, well, it’s honestly a little hard to talk about because I feel a bit silly even saying it out loud, but... well, it started a little while ago. It’s one of those modern ones with the really, really bright, built-in LED lights all around the edges? 

Anyway, ever since we put in that brighter mirror, I just... I keep noticing my face in a way I didn't before. Specifically, the skin right around my cheeks and my jawline. It just looks so uneven to me now, or kind of... saggy? Like the texture is all wrong and it's just drooping on the sides. I’ll stand there in the morning before I head to the law firm—I'm a paralegal, so I have to look put-together and professional for clients—and I just get stuck staring at how the light catches the unevenness on my jaw. 

I've even pulled my husband into the bathroom, literally pointed right at my cheek, and asked him to look at it, but he says he can’t really see what I’m talking about. He swears up and down that I look exactly the same and that he doesn't see any sagging or uneven skin at all. But I know what I'm seeing in that glass, and it's just really starting to bother me, to the point where I'm sitting at my desk at work thinking about it...

Oh, no, no, it’s really just my face. I mean, honestly, I’ve never been the type to obsess over my figure or anything like that. Sure, I’m forty-six, so obviously my body isn’t exactly what it was in my twenties, and I completely accept that. So, no, to answer your question, the rest of my body is perfectly fine, it doesn't bother me at all. I don't have any concerns from the neck down. It's really just this one specific part of my face that looks so incredibly... wrong to me now.

Well, I mean, I suppose it’s possible, logically speaking. I try to tell myself that, you know? Like I said, my husband, Jim—we've been married for eighteen years—he swears he doesn't see it. And he's usually a very observant man. If I change my hair color even a shade, he notices. So when I brought him into the bathroom and pointed right at the exact spot on my jawline under those new LED lights we installed during the mini-renovation... and he just looked at me blankly and said I looked exactly the same as I always do... part of me wanted to believe him. 

But then I look in the mirror again, and it's just so glaringly obvious to me. It's like, how can he not see that the texture is off? How can he not see that slight droop right there on the lower cheek? It makes me wonder if people are just being polite, or if they're just not looking as closely as I am. Because I know what I'm seeing. I'm not making it up. The unevenness is right there. 

I even brought a small handheld mirror into the office the other day—just a little compact one I keep in my purse—and I took it into the ladies' room at work. The lighting in there is different, more fluorescent, you know, typical office building lighting. And while it didn't look exactly the same as it does in my master bathroom with those bright, modern lights, I could still see the sagging. I could still see the way the skin just doesn't look firm anymore. 

So, yes, maybe it's not as noticeable to someone just passing me in the hallway or handing me a file, but I feel like if they really looked, if they stopped and just looked at my face for a few seconds, they would have to see it. It's just so frustrating because I feel like I'm the only one seeing this huge flaw, but it's my face, so I'm the one who has to live with it and try to cover it up every single day.

Well, a stranger on the street... I mean, I think about that a lot, actually. Like when I'm walking from my car to the courthouse for work, or just running into the grocery store to grab a few things for dinner. A stranger isn't looking at me with the eyes of a husband who's loved me for eighteen years and is just used to my face. They're seeing me exactly as I am right in that moment. 

Now, would they stop me on the street and point it out? No, of course not. People are usually wrapped up in their own worlds, looking at their phones or rushing to get their morning coffee. But if they just happened to glance up, especially if the sun is hitting my face at a certain angle—because natural sunlight can be incredibly unforgiving, honestly almost as bad as those new LED lights we installed—I really do think they would notice it. They might just think, "Oh, she looks tired," or "Her face looks a bit bottom-heavy," and keep walking. But yes, I do think they'd see the sagging. It’s just... it's hard to shake the feeling that they see exactly what I see in that bright mirror, even if Jim swears up and down that he doesn't.

Well, yes, I do think it's accurate. I mean, mirrors don't lie, do they? They're just glass and light. I know I keep bringing this up, and I probably sound like a completely broken record today, but... well, like I said before, I'm literally only here in this office talking to you because ever since we put in that brighter bathroom mirror, I just keep noticing the skin around my cheeks and my jaw. It just looks so uneven and kind of saggy to me. 

And the thing is, we specifically bought a high-quality mirror for this renovation. We went to that specialty bath store out on Route 9, not just some cheap thing from a big box discount store, because we wanted everything in the master bath to be perfect. So when I look into it, I feel like I'm finally seeing the absolute truth. I'm seeing exactly what's there in high definition, with nothing hidden. 

I know Jim says he can't really see what I'm talking about. He'll be standing right next to me, brushing his teeth and getting ready for work, and I'll point right at the exact spot on my jawline, and he just swears he doesn't see any sagging at all. He tells me I'm imagining things. But, you know, he's my husband. He's looking at me with love, not with an objective eye. He's used to my face, and he's not inspecting it the way I am. But the mirror doesn't have feelings, it just reflects the reality of the situation. So, yes, even though Jim doesn't see it, I really do believe that what I'm seeing—that unevenness and the sagging—is exactly how I actually look. It's just that our old, dim, yellow-tinted vanity lights were probably just hiding it from me all these years.

If I didn't have access to mirrors? Gosh... that's a really interesting question. I mean, obviously, the bathroom mirror is the main culprit, like I was saying before with those terrible LED lights Jim put in. Oh my goodness, the firm is always taking these casual pictures for their social media pages or the monthly newsletter—they love doing these "candid" shots of everyone working or celebrating someone's work anniversary—and I have started completely avoiding them. So, even if you took away all the mirrors... I think I'd still be worried about it, because I'm already doing all these other things, the extra makeup, the comparing, dodging the camera... it's just become this whole routine, you know? Ever since we put in that new, brighter bathroom mirror during the renovation, I just can't stop noticing how the skin around my cheeks and my jaw looks so uneven and, you know, kind of saggy to me. \n\nAnd because I see it so clearly every single morning in that mirror before I leave the house, I feel like... well, I feel like everyone else must be able to see it too, even complete strangers. A stranger isn't looking at me with the eyes of a husband who's loved me for eighteen years and is just used to my face. So, yes, even though Jim doesn't see it, I really do believe that what I'm seeing—that unevenness and the sagging—is exactly how I actually look. It's just that our old, dim, yellow-tinted vanity lights were probably just hiding it from me all these years.\n\nDoctor: Do you notice the unevenness and sagging on your face at night, after you've been out of the bright bathroom light for a while?\n\nPatient: Well, at night... you know, that's an interesting question because I really do spend so much time thinking about how the light affects things. But, honestly, even when I'm out of that bathroom, even when I'm just sitting in the living room watching TV with Jim after dinner, with just the warm, soft light from those lamps we got at Pottery Barn—the ones with the amber glass bases, which give off such a forgiving glow compared to the bathroom—I still know it's there. \n\nI mean, do I notice it exactly the same way I do when I'm standing two inches from the LED lights? Maybe not quite as sharply. Like, I'm not staring directly at my reflection while we're watching Jeopardy. But I can feel it. I can feel the weight of it, if that makes sense. I'll be sitting there, and I'll just sort of casually rest my hand on my chin or my jawline, and I can just feel that the skin isn't taut. I can feel the unevenness under my fingertips. \n\nAnd then, of course, if I get up to go to the kitchen to get a glass of water, or if I have to run upstairs to grab a sweater because the AC is turned up too high—Jim always keeps the house freezing at night—I'll catch a glimpse of myself in the hallway mirror or the reflection in the microwave door. And even in that dim light, my mind just goes right back to it. I know exactly where the sagging is, so my eyes just dart right to those spots on my cheeks and my jaw. It's like I can't unsee it, no matter what room I'm in or what time of day it is. So, even though the lighting is totally different and much darker at night, the awareness of it never really goes away. It just sort of sits there in the back of my mind, ruining my evening, honestly.\n\nDoctor: Have you considered the possibility that the unevenness and sagging you see in your face might not actually be there?\n\nPatient: Have I considered that it might not be there? Well... I mean, I guess, logically, I have to at least entertain the thought, right? He thinks I'm making a mountain out of a molehill. So, because he says that, yes, I do sometimes stop and try to think about it objectively. Maybe the sagging isn't actually there.\" I'll literally step away from the sink, take a deep breath, and try to convince myself that my mind is just playing tricks on me, or that the lighting is just casting weird shadows. I really do try to consider it. But then... I don't know, I just end up right back in front of that glass, leaning over the counter, and the evidence is just staring me right in the face. I see the unevenness. It’s so undeniably obvious to me. So even though I try to consider the possibility that it's not real, just to give Jim the benefit of the doubt and to make myself feel better, I just can't seem to actually believe it.
